Synopsis:
A dispute in Cairo over reverse-vending recycling machines (exchanging bottles/cans for phone credit) exposed deep tensions between modernization efforts and the entrenched informal waste-collection network of the "zabaleen." The zabaleen — a largely Coptic Christian community handling ~50% of Cairo's waste with ~80% recycling rates — opposed the machines' expansion into residential districts, fearing loss of livelihood. A local resolution was reached allowing zabaleen to empty the machines themselves. The broader story highlights Cairo's fragmented waste management system, the recurring failure of top-down reforms that ignore informal networks, and ongoing efforts (World Bank-funded facility, private ventures like ZeroPrime) to modernize Egypt's waste chain.
